analysis.one_liner: Lets the government license patented medicines without the patent holder's consent during public health emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in the House and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend patent law to let the Secretary of Health and Human Services authorize the use of a patented health-care invention without the patent holder's permission when the Secretary decides it is needed to address a public health emergency. The patent holder would be paid "reasonable remuneration," and the Secretary would weigh factors like the cost of developing the invention, how much publicly funded research went into it, and the public's interest in access and lower prices. It would also allow the government to license patents to export medicines needed for global health emergencies, so long as the patent holder's rights are respected in the destination market.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary patients and working families, who would gain faster access to needed drugs, vaccines, and medical devices during a health emergency at prices set with the public's interest in mind rather than a patent monopoly. Governments responding to emergencies, including shortages in other countries, would also gain a legal tool to get medicines produced. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers who could be licensed to produce the inventions would gain a new market opportunity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, governments, and generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: During a declared public health emergency, the Secretary of Health and Human Services could authorize others to use a patented health-care invention without the patent holder's consent, ending the patent holder's exclusive control over supply when the invention is needed to address the emergency.

The patent holder would still be paid reasonable remuneration, but the Secretary must weigh the public's interest as patients and payers, the benefits of expanded access and lower costs for working families and retirees, any anti-competitive practices, and how much the invention benefited from publicly funded research.

The Secretary could also authorize use of a patent to export medicines needed for global public health emergencies, provided the patent holder's legitimate rights are protected in the export market, opening a path to ship affordable medicines abroad under international trade rules.

analysis.who_pays: Patent-holding drug and device makers, who would lose the exclusive right to control production and pricing of a patented invention during an emergency, collecting court- or agency-set compensation instead of monopoly profits. They would also face competition in export markets for emergency medicines.

drawbacks.text: Companies argue that if a patent can be taken during an emergency for compensation set by the government, the reward for investing in developing new drugs and vaccines shrinks, which over time could mean fewer new medicines. The bill itself acknowledges this by requiring the Secretary to weigh "the need for adequate incentives for the creation and commercialization of new inventions."

The bill gives one cabinet officer broad discretion to decide both when an emergency justifies taking a patent and what "reasonable" pay the patent holder receives, with few procedural guardrails in the text, which critics could see as unpredictable treatment of property rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but conditional: it only matters during a declared emergency, when a patented medicine is genuinely needed and in short supply. The cost is to patent holders' exclusivity, and the strongest objection — that weaker patent rights could slow future drug development — is legitimate but partially answered by the bill's requirement to pay remuneration and to weigh innovation incentives. The measure is narrowly drawn and pays patent holders, so it does not abolish patent rights; it makes them yield in emergencies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2005, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and in February 2006 sent to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, where it stayed with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio introduced the bill on October 20, 2005, the sole sponsor, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day it was introduced.
On February 6, 2006, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution; no further action was taken, and it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patent-holding pharmaceutical and medical-device companies kept full exclusive control over their inventions, since no compulsory-licensing authority was created. No emergency-related licensing change took effect, so patients gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 20, 2005; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; it was instead sent to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, where it stalled without any markup or vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on the Constitution, House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on February 6, 2006 and held the bill for the rest of the Congress without action.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill never advanced far enough for the record to show where members stood.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug and device makers (patent holders)
industries.note: The bill would let the government license their patents during health emergencies for government-set remuneration instead of monopoly pricing, and would permit licensed exports of emergency medicines. Their interest in keeping exclusive pricing control runs against patients who would gain access and lower prices.

A compulsory-license authority would let these manufacturers produce patented medicines during emergencies without negotiating with patent holders, giving them new production opportunities while expanding patient access.
